The Battle of Malka or Battle of Balyksu took place in 1641 between two large coalitions of the North Caucasus. On one side stood the princes of Kabardia allied with the Tsardom of Russia, supported by the Nogais, the Chechens, the Shamkals of Tarki and the Endirey principality. Their opponents were the pro-independent princes of Great Kabardia led by Aleguko Shogenukov, supported by several clans of Little Nogai.
History
Prelude
Before the battle, tensions sharply escalated between the pro-Muscovite circle of Kabardian princes and their opponents. The Shamkhal of Endirey, Aidemir I, entered the conflict alongside the Tarki Shamkhalate. His brothers, Kazanali and Mamudaley, initially joined the coalition opposing Aleguko, but soon defected to the Great Kabardian side, weakening the cohesion of the anti-Aleguko force.
Course of the battle
The armies met near the Malka River. The pro-Muscovite coalition was led by several prominent rulers, including Buday I Shamkhal, Surkhay I, Aidemir I, and the Russian commander A. Shishmarev, who arrived with a detachment of Russian streltsy.
Aleguko’s forces, strengthened by Nogai allies, attacked decisively. Contemporary accounts describe the battle as a complete rout of the pro-Muscovite army. Many commanders of the Shamkhalate were killed, including Buday I, Surkhay I, Aidemir, and Muhammad Shamkhal. The Russian detachment suffered heavy losses, and its commander Artemy Shishmarev was killed.
Several Kabardian nobles of the opposing faction were taken prisoner, including Tatarhan Cherkassky, Ahlov Aytekov, and Kudenet of the Buraq (Baragun) clan. Others fled the battlefield.
Aftermath
The victory at Malka significantly strengthened Aleguko’s authority within Great Kabardia and reduced the influence of Moscow-aligned Kabardian rulers. The Shamkhalate of Tarki and the Endirey principality experienced a severe political setback due to the loss of many high-ranking nobles.
